The IMSS-BIENESTAR rules were mandatory within the program’s operating area but expressly subject to annual budget availability; the cited passages do not prove practical enforcement or effective remedies.","Jóvenes Construyendo el Futuro’s monthly evaluations and workplace visits are government-reported operational controls, not verified evidence that social commitments were enforceable. The answer qualifies the performance reporting but still gives this evidence more weight than its source permits."],"material_omissions":["The full index contains direct 2023 monitoring showing that 19% of priority programs lacked results-oriented purposes, half measured results adequately, and only six of sixteen had adequate component-purpose linkage (BATCH-0052-E006/E008). These more granular findings should supplement the aggregate 69%/50%/38% figures.","The answer omits the directly relevant finding that only 47% of six-year social-program indicators showed important progress while 53% were insufficient or lagging (BATCH-0054-E005).","It omits CONEVAL evidence that budget allocation had almost no relationship to effective target compliance and that the large health program performed deficiently (BATCH-0051-E026), which is important to distinguish funding priority from executable commitment.","It omits concrete governance risks bearing on propaganda, patronage, and administration: reported corruption in López Obrador programs and the replacement of targeted Prospera (BATCH-0012-E016/0031-E015), Segalmex diversion findings (BATCH-0007-E003, BATCH-0011-E001, BATCH-0046-E008), and evidence that some cash programs were vulnerable to patronage (BATCH-0013-E009/E013).","It omits the end-2023 pension evidence of about 11.8 million beneficiaries and associated budget trajectory (BATCH-0050-E004), which has better period fit than the 2022 pension figures used.","The conclusion could more explicitly separate welfare as a core declared and budgetary purpose—which is strongly supported—from the question’s stronger test of enforceable, politically neutral commitments, for which the record remains incomplete." ]},{"question_id":"6B.2","factual_support_1_to_5":4,"completeness_1_to_5":3,"balance_1_to_5":5,"attribution_and_period_1_to_5":5,"judge_usefulness_1_to_5":4,"material_errors":["The statement that health deprivation reached 66.8% in the lowest income decile is supported by BATCH-0032-E009, but another cited CONEVAL passage reports 66.7%; the answer should acknowledge this rounding/source-version discrepancy rather than present one value as uniquely exact.","“Access gains were real” is broader than the evidence warrants. Pension receipt, transfer income, and reductions in measured food and housing deprivation are supported, but the answer itself recognizes that nationwide service access, quality, and uptake were not established.","The discussion of migrant and asylum services is relevant to vulnerable populations but is peripheral to the enumerated health, education, water, sanitation, housing, food-security, and social-protection domains. Its prominence displaces stronger domain-specific evidence.","The phrase “selected social-protection and administrative initiatives” blurs government delivery with UN- or donor-supported outputs. BATCH-0052-E010 and BATCH-0015-E017 explicitly involve joint or international support and do not establish federal delivery alone."],"material_omissions":["Sanitation is not substantively assessed. The answer notes the gap but does not use available housing-services evidence, including declining drainage deprivation and severe rural water/drainage deficits among people in extreme poverty (BATCH-0032-E004; BATCH-0053-E010).","It omits direct 2023 or near-period education evidence from the full index: 6,390 schools implementing learning-recovery strategies (BATCH-0052-E017), the government-led Learning Camps initiative and measured literacy/numeracy gains (BATCH-0041-E007), and continuing severe proficiency and completion gaps (BATCH-0046-E007).","It omits concrete health-budget execution evidence: persistent under-execution of approved health investment and declining small clinics serving poorer communities (BATCH-0048-E010), as well as discretionary divergence from approved budgets (BATCH-0045-E011). These are central to the question’s executed-budget requirement.","It omits CONEVAL’s finding that almost all people seeking medical attention received it, while the public/private shift and catastrophic spending worsened (BATCH-0032-E010). Including both facts would sharpen the distinction between obtaining some treatment and affordable public access.","It omits territorial food-security incidence, including substantially worse 2022 deprivation in rural areas and states such as Tabasco, Guerrero, and Oaxaca (BATCH-0032-E011).","It omits the directly relevant finding that 45.1% of people in extreme poverty reported no monetary social program in 2022 (BATCH-0053-E008), a major limitation on uptake and inclusion.","It omits program-specific administration evidence for Sembrando Vida—clear selection rules and technical support alongside supply, infrastructure, banking, planning, and outcome-indicator weaknesses (BATCH-0048-E009).","The housing analysis relies mainly on deprivation trends and a single displacement case; it does not assess affordability, production, executed housing budgets, or nationwide uptake, and should state that those dimensions are unresolved rather than imply balanced domain coverage." ]},{"question_id":"6B.3","factual_support_1_to_5":4,"completeness_1_to_5":2,"balance_1_to_5":5,"attribution_and_period_1_to_5":5,"judge_usefulness_1_to_5":4,"material_errors":["The opening assertion that the administration “enacted and funded some protections for vulnerable groups” is only partially demonstrated. Funding is clear for the older-adult pension and migrant-child facilities in earlier years, but the cited IMSS-BIENESTAR and migrant-child rules establish design and authority, not adequate group-specific funding or enforcement.","The municipal pension comparison is described as the “beneficiary share” being below the “share of older people in poverty.” The exact source describes a ratio of the participation shares of beneficiaries and the target population in poverty; this is a useful mismatch indicator but not a direct coverage rate or proof that poor older people were individually excluded.","The phrase “disability affected 8.7 million people” is imprecise. The source estimates that 8.7 million people reported a disability; disability should not be characterized as an adverse event that “affected” them.","The answer places a climate-displacement case under poor and rural regional protection without clearly distinguishing Amnesty’s reported allegations about shelter treatment from independently verified findings."],"material_omissions":["The answer omits direct 2023 favorable legal developments for marginalized groups: nationwide same-sex marriage, simplified gender-marker procedures in 21 states, disability-rights reforms recognizing legal capacity and accessible shelters, and ratification of the Inter-American Convention on Older Persons (BATCH-0003-E007/E013). These are material enactment evidence even though implementation gaps remained.","It omits the direct 2023 CNDH assessment of inadequate accessible publications, cataloging, staff knowledge, and inclusion for people with disabilities (BATCH-0041-E004), as well as low compliance with recommendations on accessible health and emergency services (BATCH-0048-E011).","It omits the 2023 budget evidence for violence-against-women programs: only small real increases or a real cut, with combined funding dwarfed by the Maya Train allocation (BATCH-0041-E003). This directly bears on whether women’s protection was adequately funded.","It omits the finding that transfers declined for groups other than older adults, especially poor women, while the largest pension-coverage increases accrued to non-poor men and women (BATCH-0048-E013). This is central incidence evidence.","It omits the finding that 45.1% of people in extreme poverty received no monetary social program and that nonrecipients had worse health and food deprivation (BATCH-0053-E008).","It omits disability-program coverage distortion: the reported increase from roughly 15% to 65% largely reflected a 74% reduction in the defined target population (BATCH-0051-E025). This is highly material to targeting and exclusion.","It omits the direct 2023 allocation split showing only 4% of priority-program funds classified for people with disabilities, 6% for children and adolescents, and 1% for vulnerable populations, compared with 52% for older adults (BATCH-0052-E003).","It omits direct evidence about poor-region targeting frameworks: the 2023 poverty and social-lag report used disaggregated and geospatial information to guide FAIS infrastructure spending and required quarterly reporting (BATCH-0012-E001/E003).","It omits evidence that Indigenous and Afro-descendant identity was usually not collected in migrant-child records, obstructing group-specific incidence and protection assessment (BATCH-0015-E005/E007).","It omits the SIPINNA consultation evidence that 75% of migrant children said their opinions were not requested and many did not recall medical review or explanation of status (BATCH-0015-E006), which is more direct incidence evidence than institutional design alone.","It omits 2023 UN-supported outputs for migrant children, women, refugees, and displaced people (BATCH-0015-E012/E013/E016), which should be included with careful attribution to joint government-partner action.","Poor regions, women, Indigenous people, disabled people, children, and migrants receive some treatment, but minorities broadly, Afro-Mexicans, LGBT+ people, and several marginalized populations receive little or no systematic incidence analysis." ]}],"verdict":"pass_with_corrections","strengths":["All three answers distinguish formal rules, approved budgets, operation, uptake, and outcomes more carefully than a simple program-counting approach.","The answers consistently preserve causal and institutional attribution limits, including pandemic, subnational, agency, donor, demographic, and external influences.","Contrary evidence is prominent rather than buried: health-access deterioration, weak targeting, program-design shortcomings, service overload, gender violence, and territorial exclusion are addressed.","Period limitations are stated clearly, especially the reliance on 2021–2022 outcomes for a 2023 assessment.","Most quantitative claims checked against the supplied exact excerpts are accurate or defensibly rounded."],"systemic_problems":["The answers do not fully exploit the complete candidate index, particularly direct 2023 legal developments, program-monitoring results, execution evidence, and subgroup incidence findings.","Formal operating rules and administrative architecture sometimes receive more evidentiary weight than verified execution, enforceability, remedies, or nationwide compliance.","Older-adult pensions dominate favorable evidence, while children, disability, Indigenous populations, poor women, LGBT+ people, Afro-descendants, and poor-region targeting receive substantially thinner analysis.","Several joint UN, donor, federal, state, and civil-society outputs are included without always keeping producer and funding attribution explicit in the main narrative.","The answers frequently acknowledge domain gaps in limitations but still offer conclusions phrased broadly across the full question scope."],"concrete_corrections_required":["Add the omitted direct 2023 evidence identified for each question, especially CONEVAL monitoring, health-budget execution, disability coverage-definition changes, women’s program budgets, and 2023 rights reforms.","For 6B.1, state separately that welfare was demonstrably a declared and budgetary priority, while portfolio-wide enforceability, political neutrality, execution, and remedies remain unproven.","For 6B.2, reduce the migrant/asylum discussion and strengthen sanitation, water, housing, education, health execution, and social-program uptake analysis.","For 6B.3, add systematic coverage of every named population group and clearly distinguish enacted rights, allocated funds, delivered services, incidence, exclusion, and enforcement.","Correct the characterization of the municipal beneficiary-to-poverty ratio so it is not read as a direct individual coverage rate.","Attribute UN- and donor-supported outputs explicitly as joint results rather than federal delivery alone.","Rephrase disability prevalence as people reporting or living with disabilities, not people “affected” by disability.","Treat Amnesty’s El Bosque shelter claims as community reports relayed by Amnesty, while separately identifying the documented stalled relocation and inadequate services."],"safe_for_judge_use":false,"rationale":"The answers are generally accurate, balanced, cautious about causation, and useful as provisional syntheses. They are not yet safe as the sole basis for a skeptical judge because the full candidate index contains several material, highly relevant items that would alter the evidentiary balance—especially direct 2023 subgroup rights reforms, program-budget incidence, women’s protection funding, disability coverage-definition problems, health-budget execution, and extreme-poverty exclusion. The necessary changes are chiefly completeness and calibration corrections rather than a wholesale factual rewrite."}
